code.title: Two's complement: 32 bits, ~x and -x - 1
code.python:
# Show an int as 32 bits; the mask cuts Python's unbounded int to 32 bits
def bits(x):
    return format(x & 0xFFFFFFFF, '032b')


for x in [5, 0, -7]:
    print("x = " + str(x))
    print("  bits     = " + bits(x))
    # ~x flips every one of the 32 bits
    print("  ~x       = " + str(~x) + "  bits " + bits(~x))
    # 2's complement rule: -x = ~x + 1, so ~x = -x - 1
    print("  -x - 1   = " + str(-x - 1))
    # The same 32 bits read without a sign
    print("  unsigned = " + str(x & 0xFFFFFFFF))

# Time O(1) per number, space O(1)

followUps:
An int goes from −2,147,483,648 (−231) to 2,147,483,647 (231 − 1), so there is one more negative value than positive values.

32 bits give 232 patterns. Half of them have the top bit 0 and half have it 1. The top-bit-0 half must hold zero as well as the positive numbers, so it covers 0 to 231 − 1. The top-bit-1 half holds only negatives, −231 to −1. Zero uses up one slot on the non-negative side, and that is the whole reason for the asymmetry. A 4-bit example shows it: the range is −8 to 7.

It returns Integer.MIN_VALUE itself, −2147483648, which is still negative.

The correct answer, +2147483648, is one more than the largest int, so it cannot be stored. Negating means flip all bits and add 1: 1000…0 flips to 0111…1, and adding 1 gives 1000…0 again. The same happens for -Integer.MIN_VALUE.

This breaks code such as Math.abs(hash) % n, which can give a negative index. Use Math.floorMod(hash, n), widen to long first, or call Math.absExact, which throws instead of returning a wrong value.

Keep the same 32 bits but store them in a wider type, so the top bit counts as +231 instead of −231.

In Java: long u = x & 0xFFFFFFFFL; or Integer.toUnsignedLong(x). For x = −7 this gives 4294967289, which is 232 − 7. Java also has Integer.toUnsignedString, compareUnsigned and divideUnsigned when you do not want to widen.

Other languages: JavaScript x >>> 0, Python x & 0xFFFFFFFF, C++ (uint32_t) x, C# (uint) x. All are O(1).

code.title: Arithmetic shift (>>) versus logical shift (>>>)
code.python:
MASK = 0xFFFFFFFF  # Python has no >>>, so mask to 32 bits first

k = 2
for x in [20, -20]:
    print("x = " + str(x) + ", k = " + str(k))
    # >> copies the sign bit into the empty places on the left
    print("  x >> k  = " + str(x >> k))
    # logical shift: read x as 32 raw bits, then shift (zeros come in)
    print("  x >>> k = " + str((x & MASK) >> k))

# After masking the loop ends; plain -20 >> 1 would stay at -1 forever
n = -20 & MASK
steps = 0
while n != 0:
    n >>= 1
    steps += 1
print("shifting -20 with >>> reaches 0 after " + str(steps) + " steps")

# lo + hi does not fit in 32 bits signed; the mask gives the Java behaviour
lo, hi = 2000000000, 2100000000
print("safe midpoint of " + str(lo) + " and " + str(hi) + " = " + str(((lo + hi) & MASK) >> 1))

# Time O(1) (at most 32 loop steps), space O(1)

followUps:
It is 15.

−1 is 32 ones. >>> moves every bit 28 places to the right and fills the left with zeros, so 28 zeros are followed by the 4 ones that are left: 0000…01111 = 8 + 4 + 2 + 1 = 15.

Compare with -1 >> 28, which is still −1, because >> fills the left with copies of the sign bit and all 32 bits stay 1. This is the usual way to pull out the top 4 bits of an int: x >>> 28 always gives a value from 0 to 15.

C++ does not need a second operator because the type of the value already decides which shift you get.

C++ has unsigned integer types. >> on an unsigned value fills with zeros (logical shift), and on a signed value it copies the sign bit (arithmetic shift; guaranteed since C++20, left to the compiler before that). So you write (unsigned) x >> k to get what Java calls x >>> k.

Java has no unsigned int type, so it had to add a separate operator. Example: with x = −20, x >> 2 is −5 and (unsigned) x >> 2 is 1073741819.

In Java the result is 8, not 0 and not 235.

For an int, Java uses only the lowest 5 bits of the shift count, so the count is taken modulo 32: 35 & 31 = 3, and 1 << 3 = 8. In the same way 1 << 32 is 1. JavaScript and C# do the same.

If you need bit 35, use a long: 1L << 35 = 34359738368 (for long, the count is taken modulo 64). In C++ shifting an int by 32 or more is undefined behaviour, and in Python 1 << 35 simply gives the big number because ints have no fixed width.

code.title: Check, set, clear and toggle bit i with a mask
code.python:
def show(n):
    return str(n) + " (" + format(n, 'b') + ")"


n = 42
print("n = " + show(n))
# Check: move bit i to position 0 and keep only that bit
print("check bit 3: " + str((n >> 3) & 1))
print("check bit 2: " + str((n >> 2) & 1))
# Set: OR with the mask turns the bit ON
print("set bit 2: " + show(n | (1 << 2)))
# Clear: AND with the inverted mask turns the bit OFF
print("clear bit 3: " + show(n & ~(1 << 3)))
# Toggle: XOR with the mask flips the bit
print("toggle bit 0: " + show(n ^ (1 << 0)))
# Common mistake: n & mask is 8 here, not 1
mask = 1 << 3
print("n & mask = " + str(n & mask))
print("wrong test (n & mask) == 1: " + ("yes" if (n & mask) == 1 else "no"))
print("right test (n & mask) != 0: " + ("yes" if (n & mask) != 0 else "no"))

# Time O(1), space O(1) for every operation

followUps:
Clear the bit first, then OR in the value: n = (n & ~(1 << i)) | (v << i), where v is 0 or 1.

n & ~(1 << i) forces bit i to 0 and leaves every other bit alone. v << i is either 0 or the mask, so the OR writes v into the empty place.

Example with n = 42 (101010): i = 2, v = 1 gives 101110 = 46. i = 3, v = 0 gives 100010 = 34. If the bit already has the value, n does not change. Time and space are O(1). If v can be any non-zero number, turn it into 0 or 1 first, for example (v != 0 ? 1 : 0).

AND the number with a mask that has ones from bit i upward and zeros below: n & (-1 << i), or the same thing written as n & ~((1 << i) - 1).

−1 is all ones; shifting it left by i pushes i zeros in at the bottom. (1 << i) - 1 is the opposite mask, i ones at the bottom, so inverting it gives the same result.

Example: n = 47 (101111), i = 3. The mask is …111000, and the result is 101000 = 40. Bits 0, 1 and 2 are cleared and bit 3 itself is kept. Time and space are O(1). For an int, i must be 0 to 31; i = 32 does not clear everything in Java, because the shift count wraps to 0.

code.title: n & (n - 1): Kernighan bit count and power-of-two test
code.python:
def show(n):
    return str(n) + " (" + format(n, 'b') + ")"


# A power of two has exactly one ON bit, so removing it leaves 0
def is_power_of_two(n):
    return n > 0 and (n & (n - 1)) == 0


start = 44
n = start
count = 0
print("n = " + show(n))
# Each round removes the lowest ON bit: one round per ON bit
while n != 0:
    nxt = n & (n - 1)
    print(str(n) + " & " + str(n - 1) + " = " + show(nxt))
    n = nxt
    count += 1
print("set bits in " + str(start) + " = " + str(count))
print("64 is a power of two: " + ("yes" if is_power_of_two(64) else "no"))
print("44 is a power of two: " + ("yes" if is_power_of_two(44) else "no"))

# Time O(number of ON bits), space O(1)

followUps:
n & -n keeps only the lowest ON bit and clears everything else, the opposite of n & (n - 1), which removes that bit.

−n is ~n + 1. Flipping turns the zeros at the right end of n into ones, and the +1 carries through them and stops at the position of the lowest ON bit. So −n matches n at that bit, has zeros below it, and is the exact opposite of n above it. The AND keeps just that one bit.

Example: 44 = 101100, and 44 & −44 = 000100 = 4. It is used to step through a Fenwick tree (i += i & -i) and to pick the splitting bit in Single Number III. O(1) time.

No. In real code Integer.bitCount is faster, and you should use it.

The JVM treats bitCount as an intrinsic: on modern CPUs the JIT replaces the call with a single POPCNT instruction. Even without that, its fallback is five fixed steps of adding neighbouring bit groups in parallel, with no loop and no branch.

Kernighan's loop runs once per ON bit: 1 round for 64, but 32 rounds for −1, with a branch each round. It is only competitive when very few bits are set. Its value is that it is easy to explain and prove, and it works in any language that has no built-in bit count. Both are O(1) for a fixed 32-bit width.

n is a power of four when it is positive, has exactly one ON bit, and that bit sits at an even position (0, 2, 4, …).

boolean isPowerOfFour(int n) {
    return n > 0
        && (n & (n - 1)) == 0        // exactly one ON bit
        && (n & 0x55555555) != 0;    // at an even position
}

0x55555555 is 0101…0101, a mask of all even positions. Examples: 16 = 10000, one bit at position 4, so yes. 8 = 1000, one bit at position 3, so no. 12 has two bits, so no. Time and space O(1). Another third test that works is n % 3 == 1, because every power of four leaves remainder 1 when divided by 3.

code.title: Single Number: XOR everything, twins cancel
code.python:
a = [4, 1, 2, 1, 2]
print("input = " + str(a))

# Start at 0 because x ^ 0 = x
acc = 0
for x in a:
    # x ^ x = 0, so the second copy of a value removes the first
    acc ^= x
    print("after " + str(x) + ": acc = " + str(acc))

# Only the value without a twin is left
print("single number = " + str(acc))

# Order does not matter: XOR is commutative and associative
# Time O(N), space O(1)

followUps:
Plain XOR no longer works, because three copies do not cancel: x ^ x ^ x = x. Count the ON bits in each of the 32 columns instead and take the count modulo 3.

Each tripled value adds 0 or 3 to a column, so what is left after % 3 is the bit of the single number.

Example [2, 2, 3, 2]: column 0 has one 1 (from 3), remainder 1. Column 1 has four 1s, remainder 1. So the answer is 11 = 3. Loop up to bit 31 so that a negative answer gets its sign bit. Time O(32·N), space O(1). The ones/twos trick does the same counting for all columns at once in a single pass.

XOR everything to get a ^ b, then use one bit where a and b differ to split the array into two groups, and XOR each group on its own.

Twins have the same bits, so both copies go to the same group and cancel there; a and b go to different groups.

Example [1, 2, 1, 3, 2, 5]: the XOR of all is 6 (110). Its lowest ON bit is 2. Numbers with that bit: 2, 3, 2, which XOR to 3. Numbers without it: 1, 1, 5, which XOR to 5. The answer is 3 and 5. Two passes, O(N) time, O(1) space.

Split the array into chunks, XOR each chunk on its own thread, then XOR the partial results together.

This is correct because XOR is associative and commutative: the grouping and the order do not change the result, and twins cancel even when they sit in different chunks. Example: [4, 1, 2 | 1, 2] gives 7 for the first chunk and 3 for the second, and 7 ^ 3 = 4.

In Java: Arrays.stream(a).parallel().reduce(0, (x, y) -> x ^ y). The same idea works across machines as a map-reduce job. Total work stays O(N); with P threads the elapsed time is about O(N / P). For small arrays the cost of starting threads is larger than the gain.

code.title: Single Number II: count bits mod 3, and the ones/twos counter
code.python:
# Method 1: for each bit column, count the ON bits and take count % 3
def by_counting(a):
    ans = 0
    for bit in range(32):
        count = 0
        for x in a:
            count += (x >> bit) & 1
        # Triples add 0 or 3; a remainder means the single number has this bit
        if count % 3 != 0:
            ans |= 1 << bit
    # Python ints are unbounded: turn the 32-bit pattern back into a signed value
    if ans >= 2 ** 31:
        ans -= 2 ** 32
    return ans


# Method 2: ones and twos together count each column 0 -> 1 -> 2 -> 0
def by_ones_twos(a):
    ones, twos = 0, 0
    for x in a:
        ones = (ones ^ x) & ~twos
        twos = (twos ^ x) & ~ones
    return ones


a = [5, -4, 5, 7, 7, 5, 7]
print("input = " + str(a))
print("count per bit, mod 3 -> " + str(by_counting(a)))
print("ones/twos counter    -> " + str(by_ones_twos(a)))

# Time O(32 * N) and O(N), space O(1) for both

followUps:
Treat each bit column as a small counter that goes 0 → 1 → 2 → 0, and store the count in two bits: twos is the high bit and ones is the low bit.

When the input bit x is 0 the state stays the same. When x is 1 the state (twos, ones) moves 00 → 01 → 10 → 00.

Read the table for ones: it becomes 1 only when it would flip to 1 (ones ^ x) and twos is 0. That gives ones = (ones ^ x) & ~twos. Then twos becomes 1 only when it would flip to 1 and the new ones is 0: twos = (twos ^ x) & ~ones.

Check with x = 1: from 00, ones = 1, twos = (0^1) & ~1 = 0, giving 01. From 01, ones = 0, twos = 1, giving 10. From 10, ones = (0^1) & ~1 = 0, twos = (1^1) = 0, giving 00.

Count the ON bits in every column and take the count modulo k; any column with a non-zero remainder belongs to the special number. This needs p not to be a multiple of k.

Values that appear k times add 0 or k to a column, so they vanish under % k. The special value adds p, which leaves p % k, and that is non-zero.

int ans = 0;
for (int bit = 0; bit < 32; bit++) {
    int count = 0;
    for (int x : a) count += (x >> bit) & 1;
    if (count % k != 0) ans |= 1 << bit;
}

Example k = 3, p = 2, [5, 5, 5, 6, 6]: column 0 count 3 → 0; column 1 count 2 → 2; column 2 count 5 → 2. Bits 1 and 2 are set, so the answer is 6. Time O(32·N), space O(1).

code.title: Single Number III: split by the lowest differing bit
code.python:
a = [1, 2, 1, 3, 2, 5]
print("input = " + str(a))

# Pass 1: twins cancel, so xr = first single ^ second single
xr = 0
for x in a:
    xr ^= x
print("xor of all = " + str(xr))

# Keep only the lowest ON bit: a column where the two singles differ
diff = xr & -xr
print("lowest differing bit = " + str(diff))

# Pass 2: twins land in the same group and cancel there
with_bit, without_bit = 0, 0
for x in a:
    if (x & diff) != 0:  # compare with != 0, not == 1
        with_bit ^= x
    else:
        without_bit ^= x
print("group with that bit    -> " + str(with_bit))
print("group without that bit -> " + str(without_bit))

# Time O(N) (two passes), space O(1)

followUps:
XOR all array values together with all the numbers 1 to n. Everything cancels except the missing number m and the duplicate d, so you are left with m ^ d, which is the two-singles problem again.

  1. xr = XOR of the array and of 1..n. This equals m ^ d.
  2. diff = xr & -xr.
  3. Split both the array values and 1..n by that bit, and XOR each group. You get two numbers.
  4. Scan the array once: the one that is present is the duplicate, the other is missing.

Example [1, 2, 2, 4], n = 4: array XOR is 5, range XOR is 4, xr = 1 (which is 2 ^ 3). Group with bit 0: 1 from the array and 1, 3 from the range give 3. Group without: 2, 2, 4 and 2, 4 give 2. 2 is in the array, so the duplicate is 2 and the missing number is 3. O(N) time, O(1) space.

Because the XOR of three numbers does not give a bit that is guaranteed to separate them.

With two singles, a ^ b is never 0, and any ON bit in it is a column where exactly one of the two has a 1, so the split always puts them in different groups.

With three singles, a ^ b ^ c can be 0: for example 1 ^ 2 ^ 3 = 0, so there is no bit to split on at all. And when a bit is ON, it only says that an odd number of the three have it: one of them, or all three. If all three have it, they all land in the same group and nothing is gained. You cannot tell the two cases apart from the XOR alone. Solutions exist but need extra tricks; in practice a hash map with O(N) space is the sensible choice.

code.title: All subsets without recursion: count a mask from 0 to 2^n - 1
code.python:
items = ["a", "b", "c"]
n = len(items)
print("items = [" + ", ".join(items) + "]")

total = 0
# Every number from 0 to 2^n - 1 is one subset
for mask in range(1 << n):
    subset = []
    bits = ""
    for j in range(n):
        # Bit j of mask is 1 -> item j is in this subset
        if (mask >> j) & 1 == 1:
            subset.append(items[j])
        bits = str((mask >> j) & 1) + bits
    print("mask " + str(mask) + " = " + bits + " -> {" + ", ".join(subset) + "}")
    total += 1
print("total subsets = " + str(total))

# Time O(n * 2^n), extra space O(n) for the current subset

followUps:
Use the loop for (s = m; s > 0; s = (s - 1) & m) and handle the empty submask 0 separately. For one mask it costs 2popcount(m) steps; added up over all 2n masks it costs 3n, not 4n.

Example m = 5 (101): the loop visits 5, 4, 1, and then 0 is added: 4 submasks = 22.

Why 3n: for every item there are three cases: not in the mask, in the mask but not in the submask, or in both. For n = 3 that is 27 pairs. For n = 15 it is about 1.4·107, fine; for n = 20 it is about 3.5·109, too slow. Extra space is O(1).

The simple way is to loop over all 2n masks and keep those whose bit count is k. The faster way is Gosper's hack, which jumps straight from one mask with k ON bits to the next larger one.

int x = (1 << k) - 1;              // smallest mask with k bits
while (x < (1 << n)) {
    use(x);
    int c = x & -x, r = x + c;
    x = (((r ^ x) >> 2) / c) | r;
}

Example n = 4, k = 2: 0011, 0101, 0110, 1001, 1010, 1100, which is 6 = C(4, 2) masks. One step from 3: c = 1, r = 4, (4 ^ 3) >> 2 = 1, so x = 1 | 4 = 5. The filter costs O(2n); Gosper costs O(C(n, k)), one step per answer.

For i from 0 to 2n − 1 use the mask g = i ^ (i >> 1). Each mask then differs from the one before it in exactly one bit.

Example n = 2: i = 0, 1, 2, 3 gives g = 00, 01, 11, 10, meaning {}, {a}, {a, b}, {b}. Every subset still appears exactly once.

Why it helps: moving to the next subset means adding or removing a single item, so a running value such as the subset sum can be updated in O(1) instead of being rebuilt in O(n). The changed bit is g ^ previous g. The whole enumeration then costs O(2n) rather than O(n·2n).

code.title: Submask loop s = (s - 1) & m, and the 3^n total
code.python:
# 4-bit picture of a mask
def bits(x):
    return format(x, '04b')


m = 13
print("m = " + str(m) + " (" + bits(m) + ")")
count = 0
# s - 1 lowers s; & m throws away the bits that are not in m
s = m
while s > 0:
    print("submask " + str(s) + " (" + bits(s) + ")")
    count += 1
    s = (s - 1) & m
# The loop stops before 0, so the empty submask is handled here
print("submask 0 (" + bits(0) + ")  <- handled separately")
count += 1
print("submasks of m: " + str(count) + " (2^3, m has 3 ON bits)")

# Count every (mask, submask) pair for n = 4
n = 4
pairs = 0
for mask in range(1 << n):
    pairs += 1  # the empty submask
    s = mask
    while s > 0:
        pairs += 1
        s = (s - 1) & mask
print("all (mask, submask) pairs for n = 4: " + str(pairs) + " (3^4 = 81)")

# Time O(2^popcount(m)) for one mask, O(3^n) over all masks; space O(1)

followUps:
Count upward and force the bits of m back on each time: for (s = m; s < (1 << n); s = (s + 1) | m).

It is the mirror image of the submask loop. Adding 1 moves to the next number, and | m puts back any bit of m that the addition cleared. Seen only through the positions that are not in m, the loop counts 0, 1, 2, … so each superset appears once.

Example n = 3, m = 1 (001): 1 → (2 | 1) = 3 → (4 | 1) = 5 → (6 | 1) = 7 → (8 | 1) = 9, which is outside, so stop. The supersets are 1, 3, 5, 7. Cost: 2n − popcount(m) steps, O(1) space.

SOS (Sum Over Subsets) DP computes, for every mask at once, the sum of a value over all of its submasks in O(n·2n) time instead of O(3n).

Start with dp[mask] = f[mask] and handle one bit at a time:

for (int i = 0; i < n; i++)
    for (int mask = 0; mask < (1 << n); mask++)
        if ((mask & (1 << i)) != 0)
            dp[mask] += dp[mask ^ (1 << i)];

After bit i is done, dp[mask] covers the submasks that differ from mask only in bits 0..i. For n = 20 this is about 2·107 steps against 3.5·109.

Use it when you only need a total (sum, count, min, max) over the submasks of every mask. Keep the submask loop when you must look at each pair, as in dp[mask] = min(dp[sub] + cost[mask ^ sub]).

code.title: Add two integers with XOR (sum) and AND << 1 (carry)
code.python:
MASK = 0xFFFFFFFF  # Python ints never overflow, so keep only 32 bits by hand


def add(a, b):
    a &= MASK
    b &= MASK
    rounds = 0
    # Repeat until there is no carry left to add
    while b != 0:
        carry = ((a & b) << 1) & MASK  # without the mask the carry never leaves
        a = a ^ b                      # sum of each column without the carry
        b = carry
        rounds += 1
    # Turn the 32-bit pattern back into a signed number
    if a >= 2 ** 31:
        a -= 2 ** 32
    return a, rounds


tests = [(5, 7), (-3, 8), (-5, -9), (1, 2147483647)]
for x, y in tests:
    total, rounds = add(x, y)
    print(str(x) + " + " + str(y) + " = " + str(total) + " (rounds: " + str(rounds) + ")")

# Time O(32) rounds at most, so O(1); space O(1)

followUps:
Subtraction is adding the negative, and multiplication is adding shifted copies; both are built on the same add loop.

Subtract: −b is ~b + 1, so sub(a, b) = add(a, add(~b, 1)). Multiply: for every ON bit i of b, add a << i.

int mul(int a, int b) {
    int res = 0;
    for (; b != 0; b >>>= 1, a <<= 1)
        if ((b & 1) != 0) res = add(res, a);
    return res;
}

Example 6 × 5: 5 is 101, so res = 6 (bit 0) + 24 (bit 2) = 30. Because ints wrap at 32 bits, negative values work too. Cost: at most 32 additions of at most 32 rounds each, so O(1) for a fixed width, or O(B2) for B-bit numbers.

It works out all the carries at the same time instead of waiting for a carry to travel from column to column.

In a simple (ripple) adder, column i must wait for the carry from column i − 1, so the delay grows with the number of bits. A lookahead adder first computes two signals per column: generate g = a & b (this column makes a carry by itself) and propagate p = a ^ b (this column passes a carry on). Then ci+1 = gi | (pi & ci), and expanding this formula gives every carry directly from the g and p values.

Example 0111 + 0001: g = 0001, p = 0110. The carry into column 3 is g0 & p1 & p2 = 1, known at once instead of after three steps. With blocks arranged as a tree the delay is O(log N) gate levels (about 6 for 64 bits) instead of O(N), at the price of more gates.

code.title: Per-bit contribution: total Hamming distance and XOR sum of all pairs
code.python:
a = [4, 14, 2]
n = len(a)
print("input = " + str(a))

hamming = 0
xor_sum = 0
# Solve each bit column on its own
for bit in range(31):
    ones = 0
    for x in a:
        ones += (x >> bit) & 1
    # A pair differs in this column when one number has 1 and the other 0
    pairs = ones * (n - ones)
    if pairs > 0:
        print("bit " + str(bit) + ": ones = " + str(ones) + ", zeros = " + str(n - ones) + ", differing pairs = " + str(pairs))
    hamming += pairs
    # Each differing pair adds 2^bit to its XOR
    xor_sum += pairs * (1 << bit)
print("total Hamming distance = " + str(hamming))
print("sum of XOR of all pairs = " + str(xor_sum))

# O(N^2) check
brute = 0
for i in range(n):
    for j in range(i + 1, n):
        brute += a[i] ^ a[j]
print("brute force XOR sum = " + str(brute))

# Time O(31 * N) instead of O(N^2), space O(1)

followUps:
Turn subarrays into pairs of prefix XORs, then count per bit. Let p[0] = 0 and p[i] = a[0] ^ … ^ a[i−1]. The XOR of the subarray from l to r is p[r+1] ^ p[l], so the answer is the sum of XOR over all pairs of the N + 1 prefix values.

For each bit, if ones prefixes have it ON and zeros have it OFF, it adds ones · zeros · 2bit.

Example [1, 2]: the prefixes are 0, 1, 3. Bit 0: ones = 2, zeros = 1, adds 2. Bit 1: ones = 1, zeros = 2, adds 2 · 2 = 4. Total 6. Check: the subarrays have XOR 1, 2 and 3, and 1 + 2 + 3 = 6. Time O(32·N); space O(1) if you keep running counts per bit instead of storing the prefixes. Use long for the sum.

Work per bit: a subarray has a bit in its AND only if every element in it has that bit. So for each bit, count the subarrays that lie fully inside a run of elements that have the bit.

Keep the length of the current run; at each element the run length is exactly the number of all-ones subarrays that end there.

long total = 0;
for (int bit = 0; bit < 31; bit++) {
    long run = 0;
    for (int x : a) {
        run = ((x >> bit) & 1) == 1 ? run + 1 : 0;
        total += run << bit;
    }
}

Example [3, 1]: bit 0 has runs 1, 2, which is 3 subarrays worth 1 each. Bit 1 has runs 1, 0, which is 1 subarray worth 2. Total 5. Check: 3 + 1 + (3 & 1) = 5. Time O(31·N), space O(1).

code.title: Production bit use: permission flags and power-of-two bucket index
code.python:
# Each permission owns one bit, so a whole set fits in one int
READ, WRITE, EXEC = 1, 2, 4


# A named helper reads better than a raw mask test in business code
def has(perms, flag):
    return (perms & flag) != 0


perms = READ | EXEC
print("perms = " + str(perms) + " (READ | EXEC)")
print("can write? " + ("yes" if has(perms, WRITE) else "no"))
perms |= WRITE   # grant: turn the bit ON
print("after granting WRITE: " + str(perms))
print("can write? " + ("yes" if has(perms, WRITE) else "no"))
perms &= ~READ   # revoke: turn the bit OFF
print("after revoking READ: " + str(perms))
print("can read? " + ("yes" if has(perms, READ) else "no"))

# Hash tables with a power-of-two size replace % by a cheap mask
hash_value, buckets = 37, 16
print("hash 37 in 16 buckets: 37 % 16 = " + str(hash_value % buckets) + ", 37 & 15 = " + str(hash_value & (buckets - 1)))

# Time O(1) per operation, space O(1): one int holds the whole set of flags

followUps:
A Bloom filter is an array of m bits plus k hash functions. It answers the question have I seen this key? using very little memory, but it can sometimes say yes for a key that was never added.

To add a key, compute its k hashes and set those k bits. To look a key up, check the same k bits: if any is 0 the key is definitely absent; if all are 1 it is probably present, because other keys may have set those bits. There are never false negatives.

The trade-off is memory against error. With n keys the false-positive rate is about (1 − e−kn/m)k. About 10 bits per key with k = 7 gives roughly 1%. Add and lookup cost O(k). Plain Bloom filters cannot delete keys. Databases use them to skip disk reads for keys that are not there.

Because the bucket index uses only the low bits of the hash, and the spread step mixes the high bits into them so they are not wasted.

The index is hash & (n - 1). For a table of 16 buckets that is just the lowest 4 bits. Keys whose hash codes differ only in the upper bits would all land in the same bucket.

Example: the hashes 0x10000 and 0x20000 both give index 0 in 16 buckets. After h ^ (h >>> 16) they become 0x10001 and 0x20002, which give buckets 1 and 2. The step costs one shift and one XOR, so it is nearly free, and it reduces collisions for poor hash functions such as float keys or values that are multiples of a large power of two.

code.title: Fixed 32-bit width: a bit-count loop that also ends for negatives
code.python:
MASK = 0xFFFFFFFF


# Count ON bits by shifting right until nothing is left
def count_ones(n):
    n &= MASK  # without this line a negative n never reaches 0 and the loop hangs
    count = 0
    while n != 0:
        count += n & 1
        n >>= 1
    return count


# Turn a 32-bit pattern back into a signed number
def to_signed(u):
    return u - (1 << 32) if u >= (1 << 31) else u


# Test the edges: 0, -1, the smallest int, the largest int
tests = [13, 0, -1, -8, -2 ** 31, 2 ** 31 - 1]
for n in tests:
    unsigned = n & MASK  # the same 32 bits without a sign
    back = to_signed(unsigned)
    print("n = " + str(n) + ": ones = " + str(count_ones(n))
          + ", unsigned = " + str(unsigned) + ", back to signed = " + str(back))

# Time O(32) per number, space O(1)

followUps:
If the value is 231 or more, subtract 232; otherwise leave it as it is.

def to_signed(u):
    u &= 0xFFFFFFFF
    return u - (1 << 32) if u >= (1 << 31) else u

A 32-bit pattern with the top bit ON stands for a negative number in 2's complement, and its unsigned reading is exactly 232 too large. Example: 0xFFFFFFF8 is 4294967288 unsigned; 4294967288 − 4294967296 = −8. 0x7FFFFFFF stays 2147483647.

A one-line form without a branch is (u ^ 0x80000000) - 0x80000000. Both are O(1). Do this once at the end, after all the masked work is finished.

Yes. Any pair where the two languages disagree about integer width, overflow or shifting has the same kind of trap.

  • Java → JavaScript: bit operators use 32-bit ints, but numbers are doubles. a * b does not wrap (use Math.imul), a + b needs | 0 to wrap, and Java long masks need BigInt. Example: 1 << 31 is −2147483648; use >>> 0 to read it as unsigned.
  • Java → C++: signed overflow and shifting by 32 or more are undefined behaviour, not wrap-around. Use uint32_t or unsigned for bit work.
  • C++ → Java: there are no unsigned types, so >> on unsigned must become >>>.
  • Python → anything: big-number code silently overflows a 32-bit or 64-bit type.

The same edge tests catch all of them: 0, −1, the smallest and the largest int.
